docs.title: Development
docs.text:
From the repository root, install dependencies:

./setup.sh

Use two terminals to start the full stack:

  1. Start Redis, the Cloud API, and Celery:

bash ./scripts/launch-cloud-dev.sh

  1. Start the local engine and Tauri:

bash ./launch.sh

Set the environment variables in the Cloud API developer setup before starting the first terminal. The Cloud API is available at http://127.0.0.1:8000; the local engine is available at http://127.0.0.1:8001.

For packaged builds, see the release instructions in the repository root: distribute.sh for Linux and distribute-windows.ps1 for Windows.

docs.title: Nolain Data Query — Getting Started (Users)
docs.text: Welcome! This guide explains how to get your API key and start querying your data with the Nolain desktop app.

docs.title: Step 1 — Create an Account on the Nolain Portal
docs.text:
1. Go to nolain.app (the portal).
  2. Click Sign Up and create your account with your email address.
  3. Verify your email.

docs.title: Step 2 — Generate Your API Key
docs.text:
1. Log in to the portal.
  2. Navigate to Dashboard → API Keys.
  3. Click Generate New Key.
  4. Copy the key — it will only be shown once. Store it in a safe place (e.g. a password manager).

Your key looks like this:

sk-free-3f9a1c72b4de5e01

Keep your key private. Anyone with your key can spend your credits.

docs.title: Step 3 — Enter Your API Key in the Desktop App
docs.text:
1. Open the Nolain Data Query desktop app.
  2. In the sidebar, click ⚙️ Settings.
  3. Paste your API key into the API Key field.
  4. Click Save. The app will validate your key and show your plan and usage.

Your key is stored locally on your machine — it is never sent anywhere except to the Nolain API server when you make a query.

docs.title: Step 4 — Start Querying
docs.text:
1. Click Local Parquet in the sidebar to select a data file (.parquet or .csv).
  2. Type a natural language question in the query bar, e.g.:

What is the total revenue by country?

  1. Press Enter or click Execute.
  2. Results appear instantly in the table below.

docs.title: Plan Limits
docs.text:
Plan Credits / month Price Free 1,000 Free Premium 50,000 (see portal)

When your credit balance reaches zero, you'll see a message like:

"No credits remaining on your account. Subscribe or top up at the portal to continue using the Cloud API."

To add credits, visit Account → Subscription or Top Up on the portal.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Can I have multiple API keys? Yes — you can generate multiple keys from the portal. They all spend the same account credit balance.

What happens if I lose my key? Go to the portal, deactivate the old key, and generate a new one. Paste the new key into the desktop app settings.

Is my data sent to the cloud? Only the column names and your natural language query are sent to the cloud to generate the computation plan. Your actual data files never leave your machine.

docs.title: Credits — what you pay and what you get
docs.text: This page is for users and customers. Technical billing internals live in BILLING.md.

docs.title: How credits work
docs.text:
• 1,000 credits = $1 of model usage (1 credit = $0.001).
  • Token credits track actual model token consumption at that rate (rounded up).
  • Surplus credits are a configurable fraction of token credits (default 100%).
  • Every LLM call is charged as soon as it completes — intent classification, semantic analysis, code generation, DAG compilation, visualization, synthesis, etc.
  • Failed or cancelled jobs still cost credits for LLM calls already made.

docs.title: How much do you start with each month?
docs.text:
Credits reset on the UTC calendar month.

Plan Credits at the start of each month Approx. dollar value Free 1,000 $1 Premium 50,000 $50 Top-ups Added when purchased do not expire at month end

Your balance appears in the desktop app Settings panel and on the website.

docs.title: What one LLM call costs
docs.text:
token_credits = ceil(model_cost_usd × 1000)
surplus_credits = ceil(token_credits × surplus_rate)    # default surplus_rate = 1.0
charged_credits = token_credits + surplus_credits

With the default surplus rate of 100%, total cost is roughly 2× token credits (e.g. 3 token credits + 3 surplus = 6 charged).

Part Meaning Token credits Actual model usage (1 credit ≈ $0.001 of tokens), rounded up Surplus credits Platform margin as a fraction of token credits (default 100%)

docs.title: Observed full-query examples
docs.text:
The benchmark report contains three 50-query runs. These totals include every worker LLM call, so they are not the price of one individual call:

  • GPT-5.6 Luna, Pandas only: 4.08 credits average.
  • DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731, Pandas only: 2.76 credits average.
  • GPT-5.6 Luna, Pandas plus DAG: 38.84 credits average.

See the benchmark report for the full method, ranges, retries, and limitations.

A full successful query often involves multiple LLM calls (intent, semantics, code, optional DAG/chart). Job status shows accumulated billing.charged_credits.

On the Free plan (1,000 credits/month):

  • ~245 GPT-5.6 Luna Pandas-only answers in the measured run, or
  • ~26 GPT-5.6 Luna Pandas-plus-DAG answers in the measured run, or
  • A different amount depending on the model, question, and retries

Premium (50,000 credits/month) provides 50× the Free-plan credits. These are rough estimates, not a guaranteed number of questions.

docs.title: Other models
docs.text: More expensive models produce higher token credits; surplus scales with them. The benchmark report records measured results for specific models and run configurations.

docs.title: What is free
docs.text:
• Off-topic, explanation, and metadata replies that do not call an LLM
  • Reading task status for a job already started

docs.title: What is not free
docs.text: • Any endpoint or workflow step that invokes an LLM (conversation, generation, analyze_query, synthesis, etc.)

docs.title: Buying more credits
docs.text: Premium plans and top-up packs are sold through Stripe. Purchased credits add to your balance after payment.

docs.title: Authentication Setup Guide
docs.text: Step-by-step configuration for Google OAuth + Supabase Auth and the nolainquery portal (API key management at /account).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Component Role Supabase Auth Handles Google sign-in, issues JWT access tokens Supabase Postgres Stores profiles_nolain_query and links clients_nolain_query (API keys) to users Cloud API (/api/auth/*) Validates Supabase tokens, creates/revokes API keys Website (nolainquery-website) Login page (/login) and account dashboard (/account)

Flow:

  1. User clicks Continue with Google on /login.
  2. Supabase redirects through Google OAuth and back to /account.
  3. The website sends Authorization: Bearer <access_token> to the Cloud API.
  4. The API validates the token with Supabase and reads/writes keys in the clients_nolain_query table.

docs.title: 1.1 Create or open a project
docs.text:
1. Go to https://supabase.com/dashboard.
  2. Create a new project (or use your existing one for the Cloud API).
  3. Wait for the database to finish provisioning.

docs.title: 1.2 Run database migrations
docs.text:
In SQL Editor, run these files in order:

  1. cloud_api/sql/001_create_clients.sql (if not already applied)
  2. cloud_api/sql/002_auth_users.sql
  3. cloud_api/sql/003_account_balance.sql

This creates:

  • public.profiles_nolain_query — one row per auth user, including credit_balance
  • clients_nolain_query.user_id — links API keys to users
  • credit_balance_ledger_nolain_query and credit RPCs
  • A trigger that auto-creates a profile on sign-up

docs.title: 1.3 Copy API credentials
docs.text:
Go to Project Settings → API and note:

Setting Used by Project URL Cloud API + website anon public key Website only (safe in browser) service_role secret Cloud API only (never expose)

docs.title: 2. Google Cloud Console (OAuth)
docs.text: Google Sign-In for Supabase requires a Web application OAuth client created in the Google Cloud Console. Google does not expose this client type via gcloud or REST API — the Console UI is the only supported path (API-created clients are IAP-only and will not work with Supabase).

docs.title: Quick path: run the helper script
docs.text:
From the repo root (requires a browser on your machine):

# Refresh gcloud first if you use it for project detection:
gcloud auth login

# Opens the right Console + Supabase pages and prints your redirect URI:
./cloud_api/scripts/setup-google-oauth.sh

# Or pin a specific GCP project:
GCP_PROJECT=nolainquery ./cloud_api/scripts/setup-google-oauth.sh

The script reads SUPABASE_URL from cloud_api/.env and prints the exact redirect URI:

https://<your-supabase-ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback

docs.title: Manual path: detailed click-by-click guide
docs.text: Use this if you prefer the Console directly, or the script cannot open your browser.

docs.title: 2.1 Choose or create a Google Cloud project
docs.text:
1. Open Google Cloud Console.
  2. Click the project picker (top bar, next to "Google Cloud").
  3. Either:
  4. Use an existing project — select it from the list, or
  5. Create new → New project → Name: nolainquery → Create → wait ~30 s → select it.

Keep this project dedicated to nolainquery auth if possible. Do not reuse a throwaway/training project unless you are okay sharing its OAuth consent screen.

docs.title: 2.2 Configure the OAuth consent screen (first time only)
docs.text:
1. In the left sidebar, open Google Auth Platform (or search "OAuth consent screen").
  2. Direct link (replace YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID): https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/overview?project=YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID
  3. If you see "Google Auth Platform not configured yet", click Get started.
  4. App information screen: | Field | Value | |---|---| | App name | nolainquery | | User support email | Your email (e.g. the Gmail you sign in with) | | App logo | Optional — skip for now |
  5. Click Next.
  6. Audience screen:
  7. Select External (allows any Google account to sign in).
  8. Click Next.
  9. Contact information screen:
  10. Developer contact email: your email.
  11. Click Next.
  12. Finish screen:
  13. Review the summary → click Create (or Continue to dashboard).
  14. Scopes (if prompted separately):
  15. Click Add or remove scopes.
  16. Ensure these are included (they are usually added by default):
    • .../auth/userinfo.email
    • .../auth/userinfo.profile
    • openid
  17. Click Update → Save.

docs.title: 2.3 Add test users (required while app is in "Testing")
docs.text:
While the publishing status is Testing, only listed test users can sign in.

  1. In Google Auth Platform, go to Audience (left sidebar).
  2. Under Test users, click Add users.
  3. Add the Gmail address(es) you will use to test login.
  4. Click Save.

When you go to production, change publishing status to In production under Audience → Publishing status → Publish app (Google may require verification if you request sensitive scopes — email/profile/openid do not require it).

docs.title: 2.4 Create the OAuth Web client
docs.text:
1. In Google Auth Platform, open Clients (left sidebar).
  2. Direct link: https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/clients/create?project=YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID
  3. Click Create client (or + Create client).
  4. Fill in the form:
Field Value Application type Web application Name nolainquery portal

  1. Authorized JavaScript origins — leave empty. Supabase handles the OAuth flow server-side; you do not need your website origin here.

  2. Authorized redirect URIs — click + Add URI and paste exactly:

https://<YOUR-SUPABASE-REF>.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback

Find <YOUR-SUPABASE-REF> in Supabase → Project Settings → General → Reference ID, or from your SUPABASE_URL (the subdomain before .supabase.co).

Example:

https://fihkvacuiguhrhlnjscr.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback

Common mistakes: - Trailing slash (/callback/ vs /callback) — must match exactly, no trailing slash. - Using http:// — must be https://. - Putting http://localhost:5173/account here — that URI goes in Supabase, not Google.

  1. Click Create.
  2. A dialog shows Client ID and Client secret.
  3. Copy both immediately — you need them for Supabase (next section).
  4. Click Download JSON optionally as backup (store securely, never commit to git).

docs.title: 2.5 What you should have now
docs.text:
Item Example shape Used in Client ID 123456789-abc.apps.googleusercontent.com Supabase Google provider Client secret GOCSPX-... Supabase Google provider Redirect URI https://xxx.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback Google Console only

You do not add these to cloud_api/.env. The Cloud API validates Supabase JWTs, not Google tokens directly.

docs.title: 3. Enable Google provider in Supabase
docs.text:
1. Open your Supabase project dashboard.
  2. Direct link (replace ref): https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<YOUR-SUPABASE-REF>/auth/providers
  3. Click Google in the provider list.
  4. Toggle Enable Sign in with Google to ON.
  5. Paste from Google Console (step 2.4):
  6. Client ID → 123456789-....apps.googleusercontent.com
  7. Client Secret → GOCSPX-...
  8. Leave Skip nonce check off unless Supabase docs instruct otherwise for your setup.
  9. Click Save.

docs.title: 3.1 Redirect URLs (Supabase)
docs.text:
Go to Authentication → URL Configuration (https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<REF>/auth/url-configuration):

Setting Local dev Production Site URL http://localhost:5173 https://nolain.app Redirect URLs http://localhost:5173/account https://nolain.app/account

Click Add URL for each redirect. Supabase allows multiple entries — add both local and prod.

How redirects work: Google → Supabase callback (…/auth/v1/callback) → your site (/account). That is why Google only needs the Supabase URI, and Supabase needs your site URIs.

docs.title: 4. Cloud API environment
docs.text:
Edit cloud_api/.env:

# Existing
SUPABASE_URL=https://YOUR-PROJECT-REF.supabase.co
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=eyJhbGciOi...

# Portal CORS — comma-separated browser origins
CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173,http://127.0.0.1:5173,https://nolain.app

Restart the API after changes.

docs.title: Auth endpoints
docs.text:
Method Path Description GET /api/auth/me Profile + API keys + usage summary GET /api/auth/keys List active keys (masked) POST /api/auth/keys Create a free-tier key (full key returned once) DELETE /api/auth/keys/{id} Revoke (deactivate) a key

All require: Authorization: Bearer <supabase_access_token>

docs.title: 5. Website environment
docs.text:
Create nolainquery-website/.env:

VITE_SUPABASE_URL=https://YOUR-PROJECT-REF.supabase.co
VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=eyJhbGciOi...   # anon public key only
VITE_CLOUD_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000

For production (Vercel, etc.), set the same variables in your host's environment panel. Use your deployed API URL for VITE_CLOUD_API_URL.

Start the website:

cd nolainquery-website
npm install
npm run dev

docs.title: 6. Verify end-to-end
docs.text:
1. Start Cloud API: ./scripts/launch-cloud-dev.sh
  2. Start website: npm run dev in nolainquery-website/
  3. Open http://localhost:5173/login
  4. Sign in with Google → you should land on /account
  5. Click Create key → copy the key
  6. Test the key against the API:
curl -H "X-API-Key: sk-free-..." http://127.0.0.1:8000/health

docs.title: 7. Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Run 002_auth_users.sql on production Supabase
  • [ ] Google OAuth redirect URI uses production Supabase project ref
  • [ ] Supabase Site URL and Redirect URLs include https://nolain.app/account
  • [ ] CORS_ORIGINS includes https://nolain.app
  • [ ] VITE_CLOUD_API_URL points to your production API
  • [ ] Never commit .env files or expose SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY
  • [ ] Subscription and top-up tabs are UI placeholders until Stripe is integrated

docs.title: Cloud API conversation workflow
docs.text: This document describes the desktop Ask Queries conversation loop — the full path from session start through local execution and optional runtime repair. For platform architecture (Capability → Plan → Stage → Artifact), see SYSTEM_ARCHITECTURE.md. For job diagnostics, attempt logs, and credit receipts, see ../05-operations/TELEMETRY.md.

docs.title: Conversation loop
docs.text:
The desktop app uses this end-to-end path. Direct generation APIs such as POST /api/v2/generate_dag cover only steps 3–4; they do not run the runtime repair loop in steps 5–6.

1. POST /api/v1/conversation/start
     { metadata }
   → { session_id }

2. POST /api/v1/conversation/message
     { session_id, message, metadata, compile_dag?, plan_id?, ... }
   → text_response | meta_answer | clarification | generation { task_id, ... }

3. Poll GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id}
   → pandas_code, optional dag / visualization_spec,
     pandas_retries_left, pandas_retries, billing, ...

4. Execute locally (desktop sidecar, port 8001)
   → POST /execute_pandas for pandas code
   → POST /execute_dag when a DAG Artifact is present

5. POST /api/v1/conversation/result
     { session_id, pandas_code?, exec_error?, exec_result?, dag? }
   → exec ok: { status: "ok" } — result stored for follow-ups
   → exec_error and pandas_retries_left > 0:
        { status: "repairing", task_id: "..." }

6. On repairing: repeat steps 3–5 with the new task_id until local
   execution succeeds or the pandas retry budget is exhausted.

7. Optional: POST /api/v1/conversation/synthesize
     { session_id, question, result_summary, outcome, ... }
   → framed narrative for the UI

Two kinds of pandas retries use separate source budgets and share one chain-wide LLM-attempt ceiling:

Kind When Where Sandbox retry Truncated/empty code or static policy reject during cloud generation Inside the Celery job at step 3 (generate_pandas stage); spends pandas_sandbox_max_retries Runtime repair Code passes generation but fails when executed locally Step 5 → new job at step 3 (POST /conversation/result); spends pandas_max_retries

Both paths increment pandas_attempts_used and cannot exceed pandas_total_max_attempts (default 9: initial generation, its sandbox retries, and each runtime-repair job with a fresh sandbox budget). Compiler retries (max_retries in generation.yaml) remain independent.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The desktop app derives dataset metadata from the local engine (POST http://localhost:8001/data_summary).
  • Requests require a valid X-API-Key.
  • Sessions are reused until the desktop resets local state; server sessions expire after 24 hours.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
Term Role in this loop Intent Which conversation branch to take Capability Registered generator (data_analysis) once generation is admitted Plan Engine pipeline (data_analysis/pandas) Artifact Optional outputs (dag via Compile DAG; visualization_spec for charts)

descriptive / visualization / transformation are not Capabilities or Plans.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Start session
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/conversation/start
{ metadata }

Creates conversation:{session_id} in Redis. No LLM call; no credit charge.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Send message
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/conversation/message
{ session_id, message, metadata, provider?, model?, clarifications?, compile_dag?, plan_id? }

compile_dag is the Compile DAG UI toggle (optional DAG Artifact). plan_id is optional; default is data_analysis/pandas.

Without clarifications, LangGraph classifies intent:

classify intent
  |- out_of_scope                              -> text_response (no matching Capability)
  |- off_topic / inappropriate / underspecified -> text_response
  |- meta_question                             -> meta_answer
  |- explanation                               -> grounded text_response
  |- execution_feedback                        -> semantic analysis -> queue generation
  `- data_query                                -> semantic analysis
                                              |- ambiguity -> clarification
                                              |- semantic failure -> text_response
                                              `- clear -> queue generation
                                                (data_analysis / pandas Plan;
                                                 optional Artifacts from request options)

The classifier chooses intent using the registered Capabilities as prompt context. For generation intents it may suggest capability_id, plan_id, and include_visualization. Policy admits the Plan. Client compile_dag selects the DAG Artifact.

docs.title: Immediate response types
docs.text:
Response type Meaning Client action text_response Off-topic, unsafe, underspecified, explanation, out of scope, or fallback Display text meta_answer Dataset-structure question Display metadata answer clarification Ambiguous terms Resend with clarifications generation Job accepted Continue to stage 3

generation responses include task_id, capability_id, plan_id, compile_dag, and include_visualization.

docs.title: Clarification shortcut
docs.text: When clarifications is set, the graph is skipped. The server queues the pandas Plan with the current compile_dag option.

docs.title: Stage 3 — Poll generation job
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id}

The desktop app polls at ~1.5s intervals (up to ~80 attempts). When dag_status is success or failed, the job is done.

Key fields for the repair loop:

  • pandas_code — code to execute locally
  • pandas_retries_left — remaining local-runtime repair jobs
  • pandas_sandbox_retries_left — remaining in-cloud static retries
  • pandas_attempts_used / pandas_total_max_attempts — chain-level LLM-call usage and ceiling
  • generation_attempts — bounded attempt diagnostics (finish reason, category, selected profile, token usage, and outcome)
  • pandas_retries — sandbox retries already used

While the job runs, the worker may retry generate_pandas internally when a completion is truncated (finish_reason=length), empty, or rejected by static preflight. Partial length-limited code is never sent for execution.

docs.title: Stage 4 — Local execution
docs.text:
Execution runs on the desktop sidecar (port 8001), not on the cloud API:

  • POST http://localhost:8001/execute_pandas — run generated pandas code against the loaded dataset
  • POST http://localhost:8001/execute_dag — run the DAG Artifact when present

No cloud credit is charged for local execution.

docs.title: Stage 5 — Report result and runtime repair
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/conversation/result
{ session_id, dag?, exec_result?, exec_error?, pandas_code? }

After every local execution (success or failure), the client notifies the server so follow-up questions have execution context.

docs.title: Success
docs.text: When execution succeeds, the server stores the result and returns { "status": "ok" }.

docs.title: Runtime repair
docs.text:
When exec_error and pandas_code are both set, the previous generation job succeeded (status=success), and that job still has pandas_retries_left > 0, the server:

  1. Reads the remaining budget from the previous job's state
  2. Queues a new generate_pandas repair job with the failed code and error in the bounded pandas_error_history (no new classifier or semantic turn)
  3. Decrements pandas_retries_left on the new job
  4. Resets the in-cloud sandbox retry budget for that repair job, and carries attempt history plus the chain-level attempt count instead of resetting them
  5. Returns { "status": "repairing", "task_id": "..." }

The client then repeats stages 3–5 with the new task_id. If no retries remain, the server returns { "status": "ok" } and the client keeps the error.

Repair settings are selected from pandas_repair_profiles by normalized error category and retry index. All Pandas generation calls remain bounded by pandas_total_max_attempts.

docs.title: Stage 6 — Optional synthesize
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/conversation/synthesize
{ session_id, question, result_summary, outcome, ... }

Optional answer framing after a successful execution. On failure, the endpoint returns { "status": "success", "narrative": {} }.

docs.title: Branch reference
docs.text:
User case Server path Credit effect Off-topic / inappropriate / underspecified Classifier → text Charged if that path calls an LLM Meta question Classifier → metadata answer Free when no LLM is called Explanation Classifier → grounded text Charged if that path calls an LLM Out of scope (no matching Capability) Classifier or regex → text Charged if that path calls an LLM Clear data question Classifier → semantic → generation Credits per LLM call in the job Ambiguous question Classifier → semantic → clarification Credits per LLM call already made Clarification reply Bypass classify/semantic → generation Credits per LLM call in the job Execution feedback (“that looks wrong”) Always semantic → generation Credits per LLM call in the job Local pandas exec error with retries left Stage 5 → repair job Credits per LLM call in the repair job Local execution Desktop port 8001 No Cloud charge Answer framing Stage 6 synthesize Credits per LLM call

Worker LLM cost details and Plan stage lists: SYSTEM_ARCHITECTURE.md.

docs.title: Supported analysis boundaries
docs.text:
• Data questions (including charts and reshape) admit the data_analysis pandas Plan. Charts set include_visualization; they do not change plan_id.
  • Requests that no registered Capability can serve (out_of_scope) return a text message naming the available Capabilities and do not admit generation. A regex safety gate still catches forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, and anomaly detection while only data_analysis is enabled.
  • Explanation requests use saved result context and do not queue generation.

docs.title: Conversation endpoints
docs.text:
Endpoint Behavior POST /api/v1/conversation/start Create session (stage 1) POST /api/v1/conversation/message Main decision + job admission (stage 2) GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id} Poll generation job (stage 3) POST /api/v1/conversation/result Store local execution outcome; trigger repair (stage 5) POST /api/v1/conversation/synthesize Optional answer narrative (stage 6) GET /api/v1/conversation/{session_id} Read session DELETE /api/v1/conversation/{session_id} Delete session

Session read/delete does not verify session ownership by API key (current behavior).

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/cancel_task/{task_id}

Cooperative cancellation between Stages. LLM calls already completed keep their credit charges.

docs.title: Plan artifact dependency graphs
docs.text:
Each *.yaml file in cloud_api/app/generation/plans/config/ defines one Plan. Every file uses the same schema; only the entries under artifacts differ per plan.

Runtime code loads all YAML files at startup and registers graphs by plan_id.

docs.title: File naming
docs.text: Use {capability}.{engine}.yaml (for example data_analysis.pandas.yaml). The authoritative id is the plan_id field inside the file.

docs.title: Schema (same for every plan)
docs.text:
plan_id: <capability>/<engine>
terminal_stage: <stage_id>        # always runs last; implemented in Python, not listed under artifacts

artifacts:
  - kind: <artifact_kind>         # stable artifact id this stage produces
    stage: <stage_id>             # Celery stage implementation id
    depends_on: [<artifact_kind>] # direct dependencies only (may be [])

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text: Key Required Meaning plan_id yes Plan identifier (must match capability catalog) terminal_stage yes Final stage id (persists results after per-LLM credit charges) artifacts yes Ordered list of stage/artifact entries

docs.title: artifacts entry fields
docs.text:
Field Required Meaning kind yes Artifact kind produced by stage stage yes Registered stage id in the capability depends_on yes Artifact kinds that must exist before this stage runs

YAML is only for dependencies between plan stages. Do not put optional, request_option, or canvas in YAML — those are defined in Python (app/generation/plans/plan_behavior.py and the capability catalog).

There is no separate gate_stages section. Validation or other internal steps are ordinary artifacts entries; their canvas visibility is configured in code.

docs.title: Dependency matrix
docs.text:
For N artifact kinds there are N×(N−1) possible directed edges. List only direct dependencies in depends_on; the loader validates that every referenced kind appears in the same file.

Independent branches (same depends_on) run in YAML list order once dependencies are satisfied. If a dependency was requested but not produced (optional stage failed), dependent stages are skipped automatically.

docs.title: Example: internal validation stage
docs.text:
validate_dag validates the dag artifact and produces internal analysis (not a desktop view). Dependencies only:

  - kind: analysis
    stage: validate_dag
    depends_on: [dag]

Optional behavior and canvas visibility for this stage live in plan_behavior.py.

docs.title: Adding a new plan
docs.text:
1. Copy an existing YAML file and set a new plan_id.
  2. Fill artifacts with kind, stage, and depends_on only.
  3. Register stage behavior (optional flags, request options, canvas artifacts) in plan_behavior.py.
  4. Register the plan in the capability catalog.
  5. Implement any new stage ids in the capability module.

Adjusting dependencies for an existing plan requires editing YAML only. Changing optional stages or request-option gating requires editing Python only.

docs.title: System architecture
docs.text:
This document is a component catalog: services, the generation framework (Capability → Plan → Stage → Artifact), job infrastructure, and direct APIs.

It is not the design rationale or steering-policy intent. For layers, workflow, and why configured decisions exist, see SYSTEM_PHILOSOPHY.md. For the desktop chat loop, see CONVERSATION_WORKFLOW.md. For credits and charge timing, see CREDITS.md (users) and BILLING.md (developers). For job diagnostics, logs, and credit receipts, see TELEMETRY.md.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Nolain desktop app reads and executes the user's data locally. The Cloud API receives the question plus dataset metadata, selects a registered Capability, builds a Plan of Stages, produces Artifacts, and returns those Artifacts for local execution. All LLM traffic goes through OpenRouter (llm_models.yaml catalog).

The Cloud API does not receive the full data file. Metadata can contain column names, types, summary information, and sample values.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Desktop UI
  -> local Python engine (port 8001): derive metadata from the local file
  -> Cloud API (port 8000): conversation session + message
  -> Redis: session/job state; Supabase: API-key authentication/credits
  -> OpenRouter LLM calls: classify intent (IntentClassifierService), then semantic analysis if generation path
  -> Policy: validate Capability + Plan; apply optional Artifact options
  -> Celery worker: run Plan Stages (generate_pandas applies compatibility
     patches and static preflight; retries use typed adaptive policy)
  -> Cloud API status polling
  -> local Python engine: execute returned Artifacts against the local file
  -> if pandas exec fails and pandas_retries_left > 0: POST /conversation/result
     queues a repair job; desktop polls and re-executes
  -> Cloud API: optional answer framing and execution-result notification

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
Use these words only. Do not introduce parallel taxonomies.

Term Meaning Intent Conversation branch (IntentType). Decides whether to answer from metadata, refuse, explain, report out of scope, or admit generation. Not a Capability. Capability A registered generation product. Today: data_analysis. Field: capability_id. Plan An engine pipeline of Stages for one Capability. Today: data_analysis/pandas (implemented). Placeholder: data_analysis/ibis. Field: plan_id. Stage A unit that consumes and produces Artifacts (generate_pandas, compile_dag, …). Artifact A typed output (code_pandas, dag, visualization_spec). Some Artifacts are optional and are selected by request options, not by extra plan ids. Internal artifacts (visualization_validation, analysis) never reach the canvas.

Optional Artifacts (pandas Plan):

Option UI / caller Artifact compile_dag (default true) Compile DAG toggle dag include_visualization (default true) Dashboard / chart toggle visualization_spec

A dashboard is a visualization_spec Artifact. It is not a Plan (data_analysis/visualization/… does not exist).

Semantic analysis (spaCy + LLM sub-agents) runs before Capability admission. It is not a registered Capability.

docs.title: Intent classification
docs.text: The conversation graph (app/services/conversation_manager.py) starts every turn at the classify node. IntentClassifierService (app/services/intent_classifier.py) makes one LLM call to choose a conversation intent before any generation is admitted.

docs.title: Why a classifier (architectural choice)
docs.text:
Design Rationale Intent ≠ Capability Intents branch the conversation (answer from metadata, refuse, explain, admit generation). Capabilities are registered generators. Mixing them would let the LLM pick Stage graphs or invent products. Single call at entry Cheap gate: most turns are off-topic, meta, or explanatory and never reach the worker. Generation intents share one downstream path (semantic analysis → policy → Celery). Classifier suggests; server decides For data_query / execution_feedback the LLM may suggest capability_id and plan_id. Policy (app/generation/policy.py) validates against the registry, applies client Artifact toggles, and builds the Plan. Dynamic prompt catalog {available_capabilities} and {generation_catalog} are rendered from the live registry so new Capabilities appear in the prompt when registered and enabled—without hard-coding plan lists in the classifier. Client owns optional Artifacts The classifier must not set compile_dag or include_visualization. The desktop Compile DAG / Dashboard toggles (and /conversation/message fields) are authoritative. Fail-open on errors Parse or LLM failures default to data_query with routing.source="default" (data_analysis + data_analysis/pandas).

A deterministic safety gate (app/services/analysis_capabilities.py) can still override routing: wording that explicitly asks for forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, or anomaly detection routes to respond_out_of_scope even if the classifier returned data_query.

flowchart TD

  classify -->|explanation| respond_explanation[respond_explanation]

Catalog stages lists the full optional set; request options drop unused stages at admission.

Legacy plan ids (data_analysis/{analysis\|visualization\|transformation}/{with_dag\|pandas_only}) map to data_analysis/pandas plus the corresponding options.

Request options (not plan ids)

  • compile_dag (bool, default true) — produce the DAG Artifact
  • include_visualization (bool, default true) — produce the visualization_spec Artifact
  • plan_id (optional) — must be a catalog Plan; server rebuilds Stages

Retry budgets (cloud_api/app/config/generation.yaml)

Key Spent by Default max_retries compile_dag / validate_dag / format_visualization / validate_visualization retries 2 pandas_sandbox_max_retries In-cloud retries after truncated/empty output or static preflight rejection 2 pandas_max_retries Local-exec repair jobs from POST /conversation/result 2 pandas_total_max_attempts Chain-wide ceiling across initial generation, sandbox retries, and runtime repairs 9

A pandas repair selects a pandas_repair_profiles entry by normalized failure category and retry index. Surgical categories emit with reasoning disabled so hidden tokens cannot empty the completion. Truncated repair calls keep the previous actionable error as the next prompt target. The legacy pandas_repair_reasoning and pandas_repair_max_tokens keys provide the fallback profile. First-pass generation still uses the model catalog defaults in llm_models.yaml. Runtime-repair jobs reset pandas_sandbox_retries_left instead of inheriting a depleted sandbox budget. New pandas_code invalidates dag / visualization_spec; if compile_dag is on, those stages run again on the repaired code.

docs.title: Routing and admission policy
docs.text:
See Intent classification for the full intent catalog, prompt reference, and graph routing.

flowchart LR
classifier[IntentClassifierService] --> suggestion[GenerationRoutingSuggestion]
suggestion --> policy[policy.resolve_admission]
policy --> registry[registry.build_plan]
registry --> orchestrator[validate_plan]
orchestrator --> worker[Celery worker]
  1. Classifier emits intent and, for data_query / execution_feedback only, suggests capability_id and plan_id from the live catalog. It does not choose optional Artifacts or Stage graphs.
  2. Policy (app/generation/policy.py) checks the Capability is registered, resolves plan_id, and applies Artifact options. Client toggles are authoritative for optional Artifacts.
  3. The LLM never selects Stage graphs directly.

Precedence:

  • Client compile_dag on /conversation/message selects the DAG Artifact.
  • Client include_visualization selects the visualization_spec Artifact (desktop Dashboard toggle).
  • Optional plan_id must match the catalog (data_analysis/pandas today).
  • Unknown Capabilities fall back to data_analysis.
  • data_analysis/ibis is rejected until implemented.

docs.title: Celery execution
docs.text:
code_generator_task
  -> build Plan from worker config
  -> run_stage_task (stage 0)
       -> generate_pandas: apply compatibility patches, static preflight
       -> on length/empty/preflight reject: adaptive retry
          (pandas_sandbox_max_retries + pandas_total_max_attempts)
       -> optional compile_dag / format_visualization
       -> validate_visualization may retry format_visualization (max_retries)
       -> validate_dag may retry compile_dag (max_retries)
       -> finalize_plan (stop / persist)

Legacy v1 planner_task chain (POST /api/v1/generate_dag) does not use the capability registry.

docs.title: Authentication and credits
docs.text:
All workflow endpoints require X-API-Key. Conversation routes pre-check remaining credits without charging; each LLM call is charged immediately.

Portal-linked keys with an empty balance return HTTP 402. Unlinked non-owner keys return 402. Unlinked owner developer keys skip credit checks. See BILLING.md.

docs.title: Job infrastructure
docs.text:
• Queue preflight: Redis + Celery worker required (503 if unavailable)
  • Redis job_state:{job_id} — 1 hour TTL
  • Conversation conversation:{session_id} — 24 hour TTL
  • Cooperative cancellation before/after Stages
  • Status polling: GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id} — returns legacy fields plus capability_id, plan_id, current_stage, plan, compile_dag, include_visualization, optional artifacts[], and bounded generation_attempts

Useful job states include queued, generating_code, compiling_from_code, formatting_visualization, validating_visualization, validating, finalizing, charging, success, failed, cancelled, and legacy v1 states for mixed clients.

docs.title: Future capabilities
docs.text:
A second Capability (e.g. RAG) would:

  1. Implement the Capability protocol and register in app/generation/__init__.py
  2. Declare its Plans and optional Artifacts
  3. Extend policy ENABLED_CAPABILITIES
  4. Reuse shared artifact types where appropriate

The ibis Plan is the next data_analysis Plan: generate_ibis → validate_ibis. It is catalogued but not implemented.

The out_of_scope intent covers requests that no enabled Capability can serve. The classifier sees those Capabilities in its prompt; until a matching Capability is registered, the conversation graph returns a text message and does not admit generation. Explicit out-of-scope wording (forecasting, p-values, optimization, anomaly detection) is also caught by detect_out_of_scope_kind() before generation.

docs.title: System philosophy
docs.text:
This document describes what the system is, how work moves through it, which rules are load-bearing, and which decisions steer behavior (cost, quality, trust). It uses layers and product language, not services, endpoints, or config file names.

For components, contracts, and where policies are configured, see SYSTEM_ARCHITECTURE.md. For the desktop chat loop in operational detail, see CONVERSATION_WORKFLOW.md.

docs.title: The core bet
docs.text:
Nolain is a local computation product with a remote reasoning service, not a cloud analytics warehouse.

The user’s file stays on the machine that already has it. The remote side sees a sketch of the data (schema, types, summaries, samples) and returns artifacts — executable analysis, an optional computation graph, an optional chart contract — that the local engine can run. Results are true because they were computed against the real file, not because a model claimed them.

That split is the product. The workflow below is how the split is kept reliable, cheap enough, and hard to misuse.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Four layers, from closest to the user to farthest from the data.

Local layer          data, metadata, execution
Dialogue layer       whether this turn should generate anything
Synthesis layer      admitted generation → typed artifacts
Settlement layer     identity, model choice, cost of reasoning

Each layer has a job it must do, and a class of decisions it must refuse. The control plane is dialogue + synthesis + settlement (reason, admit, charge). The data plane is local (own the file, compute, report). Metadata is the only interface between them.

docs.title: Local layer
docs.text:
Responsibility. Own the file. Derive the sketch. Execute artifacts. Show results. Report what happened.

This is the only place that may touch the full dataset. It is also the only place whose output counts as an answer: a number, a table, a chart from real rows.

What it refuses. It does not invent analysis. It does not call models. It does not decide product scope. If synthesis returns nothing executable, this layer has nothing to run.

Strength. Privacy is structural, not a policy checkbox. Execution latency is local. The engine can grow without teaching the remote side about the user’s rows.

Assumption. The sketch is a good enough surrogate for the file that generated artifacts will usually run. The user (and the desktop) can be trusted to execute what comes back and to report success or failure honestly.

Tradeoff. Generation quality is capped by the sketch. Rare values and file-specific quirks that never appear in samples will surprise the model. Sending the file would raise hit rate and destroy the privacy bet.

docs.title: Dialogue layer
docs.text:
Responsibility. Treat each user turn as a conversation decision, not as a generation request. Classify intent. Answer from the sketch when that is enough. Refuse what is off-topic, harmful, underspecified, or outside enabled products. Ask for clarification when the question is ambiguous. Only then admit generation.

This layer is a gate. Most turns should never reach synthesis. That is a cost decision and a safety decision.

What it refuses. It does not pick pipelines or optional artifacts. Intent is not a product. “The user wants a chart” is not “invent a visualization product.” Optional outputs are the user’s (and the desktop’s) choices.

Strength. The conversation can be useful without a generation job: column lists, explanations of a prior result, a clear “we don’t do that yet.” New products can appear in the catalog without turning the gate into a planner.

Assumption. A cheap classification, plus a deterministic override for clearly out-of-scope wording, is enough to keep generation rare and on-product. Fail-open (treat a broken classifier as a data question) is better than silently dropping real questions.

Tradeoff. Fail-open spends money and can admit work that should have been refused. Clarification adds a turn — and a charge — before any artifact exists.

docs.title: Synthesis layer
docs.text:
Responsibility. Once generation is admitted, produce typed artifacts under a registered Capability, through a Plan. Policy rebuilds the Plan. The model fills in artifacts; it does not design the machine that produces them.

  • A Capability is a product (“descriptive analysis of one file”).
  • A Plan is an engine for that product (one implemented engine today; others may be catalogued and still refused).
  • Stages consume and produce artifacts.
  • Optional artifacts (graph, chart) are request options on a Plan, not extra products.

What it refuses. The model does not select Capabilities, Plans, or the shape of the pipeline. Unknown or unimplemented Plans are rejected. A dashboard is an artifact, not a Plan. Understanding the question (semantic analysis) happens before admission; it is not itself a Capability.

Strength. One Plan can grow optional outputs without a combinatorial explosion of products. Deterministic checks sit next to generative steps so retries have something other than “try again” to push against.

Assumption. Executable analysis is the primary artifact; the graph and the chart are projections of that analysis (and the question). Local execution plus a bounded repair loop will catch a useful fraction of mistakes without reopening the dialogue gate.

Tradeoff. Code-first means the graph can drift from what actually ran, and a chart contract can disagree with both. Repair re-generates from the failure, not from a deeper reading of the question.

docs.title: Settlement layer
docs.text:
Responsibility. Know who is calling. Offer a catalog of models. Charge for reasoning work as it happens (each model call), not for “a query” as a lump. Keep the control plane from doing work it cannot bill or should not admit.

What it refuses. This layer does not execute data. It does not decide whether a question is in scope. A caller with no portal account (except a dedicated developer credential) does not get a path through. An empty credit balance does not get another job.

Strength. One model gateway keeps the product from growing a provider-shaped codebase. Charging per call matches actual cost: a job with a graph and a chart is several calls, not one.

Assumption. Immediate settlement on each call is acceptable even when a later step fails. Users will tolerate paying for the gate, for clarification, and for failed compiles because those were real model calls.

Tradeoff. Price follows token usage, so the same question costs different amounts on different models and on retry-heavy paths. Conversation memory that lives in a short-lived store will vanish.

docs.title: How work flows
docs.text:
The system is a loop between the data plane and the control plane. The file never crosses that boundary. Artifacts and a sketch do.

Local:  load file → sketch
   → Settlement: who is this, may they spend?
   → Dialogue: open a session on that sketch
   → Dialogue: each turn → refuse | answer | clarify | admit
        ↳ if admitted: Policy rebuilds a Plan
        ↳ Synthesis: artifacts (with internal checks and bounded retries)
   → Local: execute artifacts on the file
   → Dialogue: store the outcome (follow-ups, explanations)
        ↳ if execution failed and repair budget remains:
             Synthesis again (no new classification) → Local again
   → optional: Settlement-charged framing of the result into narrative

docs.title: 1. Presence — the file becomes a sketch
docs.text:
The user loads a table on the desktop. The local layer reads it and produces a sketch: column names, types, summaries, sample values. That sketch is what every later layer is allowed to see.

Restriction. The full file does not leave the machine. If the sketch is wrong or thin, every downstream step inherits that error.

docs.title: 2. Identity — settlement before work
docs.text:
Before any conversation turn or generation, settlement asks: is this a known caller, and may they spend?

Caller Admission Charged for model work Portal-linked account with remaining credits Yes Yes Portal-linked account with empty balance No — Unlinked non-developer credential No — Dedicated unlinked developer credential Yes No

Restriction. Queueing work is not itself a charge. Every model call that does run is charged as soon as it completes, including calls that later look wasted (a compile that fails, a gate that then refuses). Local execution is never a cloud charge.

docs.title: 3. Session — dialogue binds a sketch to a thread
docs.text:
Dialogue opens a session: a short-lived memory of messages, the current sketch, and (later) the last result. No model call is required to open it.

Restriction. The session is not a durable account object. It expires. It is not a strong proof of ownership. Follow-ups and explanations are only as good as what that memory still holds.

docs.title: 4. A turn — dialogue decides the branch
docs.text:
The user asks a question. The desktop sends the message, the current sketch, and the user’s choices about optional artifacts (whether they want a computation graph, whether they want a chart). Those choices belong to the local layer / the user, not to the model.

Dialogue classifies the turn once, then branches. Classification is a model call (settlement charges it). A wording-based safety override can still force “out of product” even if classification wanted to generate.

Kind of turn What happens Reaches synthesis? Off-topic, harmful, or too vague A short refusal or a prompt for a better question No Answerable from the sketch alone (columns, row count, types) Answer from metadata; no generation No Explain a prior result or method Grounded text from stored outcome No Data-related, but no enabled Capability can serve it Named refusal (forecasting, inference, optimization, anomaly detection, and anything else the catalog cannot do) No Ambiguous data question Ask for clarification; wait for the next turn Not yet Clear data question Semantic reading of the question, then admission Yes, if still clear “That result looks wrong” Treat as a new generation with the prior question plus the feedback Yes

Restriction. A user message is not a generation request until this layer says so. The classifier may suggest a Capability and a Plan for generation turns. It must not choose optional artifacts, and it must not invent a product. Policy, not the prompt, is authoritative.

Fail-open. If classification fails to parse, dialogue treats the turn as a data question and continues toward admission. That spends money in order not to drop a real question.

Clarification shortcut. Once the user has answered a clarification, the next send may skip classification and semantic reading and go straight to admission. The question’s meaning is treated as settled.

docs.title: 5. Admission — policy, not the model, builds the Plan
docs.text:
For generation turns, a second look at the question (semantic analysis) may still stop the flow: if terms are ambiguous, dialogue asks; if that reading fails, it answers in text and does not generate.

If the question is clear, policy admits:

  1. The Capability must be registered and enabled. Unknown ids fall back to the one enabled product (descriptive analysis of one file).
  2. The Plan must be a known engine for that product. An unimplemented engine is rejected, not approximated.
  3. Optional artifacts come from the client’s toggles, not from the classifier.
  4. The server rebuilds the Plan. The model never selects the pipeline.

Restriction. There is one enabled Capability today. Everything else is out of scope until a new Capability is registered and enabled. A chart is not a different product; it is an optional artifact on the same Plan.

docs.title: 6. Synthesis — artifacts, checks, bounded retries
docs.text:
Admitted work produces artifacts under the Plan:

  1. Primary artifact: executable analysis (code) from the question and the sketch.
  2. Optional graph: a computation-graph view derived from that code, if the user asked for it.
  3. Optional chart contract: a renderer-neutral spec, if the user asked for it.

After each generative step, a deterministic check may reject the artifact (static sandbox on code; structural validation of the graph; contract validation of the chart). Rejection spends a retry budget and re-runs the generative step that produced the bad artifact. Two budgets exist and do not borrow from each other:

  • a budget for producing executable analysis (also shared with local-exec repair, below);
  • a budget for graph/chart compilation and validation.

Restriction. Synthesis does not execute the user’s file. It may only inspect the sketch and the artifacts it has already produced. Code that fails the static sandbox never ships. When analysis is regenerated, derived artifacts (graph, chart) are invalidated and must be produced again if still requested.

Settlement. Each model call inside this work is charged immediately. A failed compile still costs. Local execution, when it happens, does not.

docs.title: 7. Execution — only the local layer may compute
docs.text:
The desktop receives artifacts and runs them against the real file. That is the first moment the analysis meets the data.

Restriction. A successful job on the control plane is not an answer. The local result is. The control plane is not charged for this step.

docs.title: 8. Report and repair — execution feedback without reopening the gate
docs.text:
After every local run, success or failure, the desktop tells dialogue what happened. A successful result is stored for later explanation and follow-up.

If execution failed, and the analysis-retry budget still has remaining attempts, dialogue does not classify again. It sends the failed artifact and the error back to synthesis (a repair). The desktop waits, executes the new artifacts, and reports again, until the run succeeds or the budget is exhausted.

Kind of correction When Re-enters dialogue classification? Internal synthesis retry Artifact rejected by a static check before it ships No Runtime repair Artifact passed checks but failed on the real file No

Restriction. Repair cannot change what the question meant. It cannot spend more than the remaining budget. It cannot turn a data question into a different Capability. Graph/chart retries are a separate budget and are not spent here.

docs.title: 9. Framing — narrative is optional and after the fact
docs.text: Once a result exists, the desktop may ask for a narrative wrapping. That is another model call (charged). It must not replace the executed result. If framing fails, the user still has the numbers.

docs.title: Two entry points
docs.text:
The loop above is the conversation path (the desktop product).

There is a direct generation path: skip session and dialogue, admit a Capability from the request, run synthesis, return artifacts. That path does not classify, does not clarify, and does not run the local repair loop. It is the same product with the gate and the memory stripped off.

Restriction. Those two paths must not silently become two products. Direct generation is the same Capability and the same artifacts; it is honest about omitting the gate.

docs.title: Steering policies
docs.text:
The philosophy is not only layers and workflow. It is also explicit decisions that aim the system: what to optimize on the happy path, what to spend when something fails, and what must never be delegated to the model.

These decisions live in configuration and in code. The important part is the direction, not the knob name. Changing a steering policy is a product bet — “we now value X over Y” — not a cosmetic tweak.

docs.title: Emit fast, keep repairs executable
docs.text:
Decision. First-pass artifact generation uses minimal model reasoning. Surgical repairs — syntax, invalid unicode, sandbox policy, and runtime column/name fixes — also emit with reasoning disabled. Hidden reasoning is not spent on those paths because reasoning tokens share the completion budget and can starve the visible program.

Why. First pass is emission: turn a clear question and a sketch into executable analysis. Extra “thinking” mostly adds latency and cost without improving code that must pass deterministic checks anyway. A typo, a zero-width space, or a bad column name is still emission of a short corrected program, not open-ended diagnosis. When a repair call hits the token limit, the original actionable error is kept as the next prompt target; truncation is call metadata.

Direction. The system prefers cheap, direct generation, and pays for longer visible completions on repair rather than hidden reasoning. Deterministic fixes (strip illegal format characters, localize runtime line numbers) run before any model retry.

docs.title: Separate retry budgets
docs.text:
Decision. Retries are not one pool. Analysis has distinct budgets for (a) in-cloud rejection before anything ships, (b) local execution failure reported back, and (c) graph/chart compile and validation. Pandas calls also share a chain-wide ceiling so nested repair jobs cannot multiply total model calls.

Why. A compile loop should not consume the user’s allowance for “the code was right but my file surprised you.” A sandbox reject should not exhaust the budget for real execution feedback. Each failure mode has a different fix; lumping budgets would either starve repairs or over-spend on cheap rejects.

Direction. Failures are bounded and typed. Source budgets preserve the meaning of each retry, while the chain ceiling bounds total cost.

docs.title: Checks before ship, execution only local
docs.text:
Decision. Executable analysis is inspected on the control plane with static policy (no running the user’s data in the cloud). Graph and chart contracts get deterministic validation after generative steps. Only the local layer runs against the file.

Why. The privacy bet forbids cloud execution on full data. Static rejection catches a large class of unsafe or unusable code early. Validation gives retries a concrete error, not “try again.” Local execution is the ground truth the sketch could not provide.

Direction. Trust is staged: sketch → generated artifact → checked artifact → executed result. Each stage can send work backward; none skips straight to “believe the model.”

docs.title: Regenerate downstream when upstream changes
docs.text:
Decision. When executable analysis is regenerated (repair or sandbox retry), derived artifacts — graph, chart — are invalidated and rebuilt if still requested.

Why. Derived views are projections of the analysis. Keeping an old graph attached to new code would lie to the user about what ran.

Direction. One primary artifact anchors truth; everything else follows it or disappears.

docs.title: Model catalog vs repair profile
docs.text:
Decision. The model catalog sets defaults for which models exist, default reasoning per model, and routing preferences. Pandas repair selects a profile from the normalized failure category and retry index. Syntax, Unicode, sandbox-policy, and first runtime repairs emit compact code with reasoning disabled. A truncated repair keeps the original error as the prompt target and may raise max_tokens without turning reasoning back on.

Why. Catalog defaults optimize the common case across all call sites (classifier, semantic reading, compile, chart format). Repair is a different job with different economics; it should not inherit “fast emitter” settings.

Direction. Defaults are for throughput; evidence from the actual failure chooses the recovery budget.

docs.title: Charge the call, not the question
docs.text:
Decision. Every model invocation settles immediately when it completes. Queueing synthesis is not a charge. Local execution is never a charge. A margin (surplus) is applied on top of raw token cost.

Why. Vendor cost is per call. Hiding failed compiles or gate calls inside a flat “query price” would misalign product and infrastructure. Surplus funds variance (retries, pricing drift) without pretending one successful path defines the price of reasoning.

Direction. Users pay for reasoning work that actually happened. The product is honest that a “simple question” can be several calls.

docs.title: Gate: fail-open, then narrow
docs.text:
Decision. If intent classification breaks, treat the turn as a data question and continue toward admission. A separate wording-based safety layer can still refuse forecasting, inference, optimization, and anomaly detection. The classifier must not set optional artifacts.

Why. Fail-open favors not losing real questions over not spending on junk. The safety layer catches a small set of high-risk asks that should never reach synthesis even when classification misfires. Optional artifacts stay with the user/desktop so the gate cannot silently turn on expensive outputs.

Direction. The conversation gate is permissive on machinery failure, strict on product boundary, silent on user toggles.

docs.title: Admission is server-side
docs.text:
Decision. Models may suggest a Capability and Plan; policy rebuilds the Plan from the registry and client toggles. Only enabled Capabilities admit. Unknown Plans reject; unimplemented Plans reject.

Why. Prompts drift; registries do not. Letting the model pick pipelines would make every new product a prompt edit instead of a registration.

Direction. Extensibility through registration, not through chat creativity.

docs.title: Reasoning-capable models still emit on the happy path
docs.text:
Decision. Even when the chosen model supports extended reasoning, code and JSON emitters default to no extra reasoning effort on first pass and on surgical Pandas repairs. Heavier models in the catalog may use more reasoning for tasks that need it (e.g. explanation paths).

Why. Reasoning tokens are expensive and invisible to the user until they fail. For structured output that will be validated anyway, thinking is often waste.

Direction. Use the model’s strength for output quality and validation loops, not for open-ended cogitation on every turn.

docs.title: Where steering is configured
docs.text:
Tunable steering (source retry budgets, chain attempt ceiling, category repair profiles, model defaults, credit formula) lives in policy files loaded at startup. Structural rules (admission, failure classification, sandbox, intent routing, charge timing) live in code. The architecture doc maps file to concern; this doc maps decision to intent.

When you change a value, ask: which direction does this push? Examples:

If you increase… You are saying… Repair reasoning effort Failures deserve more diagnosis; accept higher cost on the error path Sandbox retry budget Reject early, retry often, before the user ever runs code Exec-repair budget Local truth matters; keep trying after the sketch misled generation Compile/chart retry budget Derived artifacts must be structurally valid, not just plausible Default reasoning on emitters Willing to pay latency/cost on every first pass for possibly better code Surplus rate Pricing should carry more buffer above vendor cost Fail-open → fail-closed Prefer refusing ambiguous turns over spending on possible junk

docs.title: Policies and restrictions
docs.text:
These are the rules the workflow is not allowed to “work around.” Changing them is a philosophy change.

Data

  • The file stays local. The sketch is the only remote view of the data.
  • One loaded table is the unit of analysis.
  • Enabled product: descriptive work on that table (aggregations, comparisons, rankings, trends, quality checks, reshape, optional charts).
  • Not enabled until a Capability says so: forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, anomaly detection, and anything else the catalog does not name.

Authority

  • Models propose; policy admits. Registries and client options are the source of truth.
  • Intent (conversation branch) is not a Capability (generation product). Mixing them would let a prompt invent a pipeline.
  • Optional artifacts are user/desktop toggles on one Plan, not new Plans and not classifier output.
  • Unimplemented Plans are rejected. Unknown Capabilities fall back to the enabled default; they are not invented.

Generation

  • Generation is admitted, not assumed.
  • Semantic reading of the question is a gate, not a product.
  • Executable analysis is primary; graph and chart are derived and optional.
  • Static checks must pass before an artifact ships. Execution happens only locally.
  • Fail-open on classifier failure; wording-based safety may still refuse an admitted-looking data question.

Repair and memory

  • Runtime repair is execution feedback, not a new conversation.
  • Dialogue memory is short-lived and weakly bound to the caller.
  • Cooperative cancellation may stop work between steps; model calls already completed stay charged.

Settlement

  • Charge the reasoning, not the job. Each model call settles when it completes.
  • Empty balance: no further admitted work.
  • Local execution is free to the cloud.
  • Developer credentials that are not tied to a portal account skip settlement; every other caller does not.

docs.title: Cross-cutting rules
docs.text:
Control plane vs data plane. The cloud may reason. Only the local layer may compute on the file. If the sketch is too thin, generation quality falls; if it is too thick (full rows, full files), the split collapses.

Suggest, then decide. This is how the system stays extensible without letting a prompt invent a product.

Artifacts are the contract. The desktop does not consume “a job succeeded.” It consumes executable analysis, a graph, a chart spec.

The conversation may refuse. A useful product is allowed to say no, to explain, or to answer from the sketch.

docs.title: Strengths (as a whole)
docs.text:
• Structural privacy. The file never has to be uploaded for the product to work.
  • Answers grounded in execution. The UI can show what ran, not only what was said.
  • A conversation that can refuse. Most turns never reach synthesis.
  • A small, explicit product surface. One Capability, one implemented Plan, optional artifacts.
  • Deterministic belts around generative steps. Checks give retries a target.
  • Cost aligned with work. Credits track model calls. Local execution is free.

docs.title: Assumptions (as a whole)
docs.text:
• The sketch is representative enough, often enough.
  • A single executable-analysis engine is a sufficient lingua franca between control plane and data plane.
  • The desktop is a trusted partner: it executes, it reports, it owns optional-artifact toggles.
  • Bounded retries and a fail-open gate are preferable to silent refusal.
  • Users will accept paying for the gate and for failed steps because those were real model calls.

docs.title: Tradeoffs worth naming
docs.text: Choice What it buys What it costs Sketch only, never the file Privacy, simpler trust, local truth Missed quirks; generation can be locally wrong Intent gate before generation Cheap refusals; clearer product boundary Extra calls; fail-open can admit junk Classifier suggests, policy admits The model cannot invent pipelines Catalog and policy must stay the real source of truth Optional artifacts, not extra Plans One Plan, many outputs Options must be carried on every turn; easy to document wrong Analysis first, graph and chart derived Fast path to something executable Drift between code, graph, and spec Repair without re-classifying Fast correction on exec errors Repair cannot change the question’s meaning Charge every model call immediately Matches vendor cost; no “job-shaped” fiction Users pay for failed steps and for the gate itself Short-lived session memory Simple operations History is not a durable account object Single enabled Capability Honest “out of scope” Dialogue must keep saying no Direct generation beside conversation Same artifacts without a chat Two paths that can drift if they are not kept honest

docs.title: Room for improvement
docs.text:
The current shape is a working compromise, not a finished architecture.

The sketch is still a sketch. Better summaries, better samples, and honest signals about data quality would raise hit rate without moving the file.

One Capability is both a strength and a ceiling. “Out of scope” is doing a lot of work. A second product will test whether intent, policy, and artifacts actually compose.

A second engine is a promise. Until another Plan is implemented, “Plan = engine” is vocabulary, not a proven split.

Code, graph, and chart can disagree. Treating the graph as a projection is convenient. Making it the executable source of truth would make the canvas trustworthy. That is not done.

Dialogue is a good gate and a weak memory. Sessions expire, ownership is weakly bound, and follow-up quality depends on whatever was last stored.

Fail-open and wording-based safety are temporary ethics. Admission should eventually fail closed on classifier failure. Out-of-scope should come from the Capability catalog, not from phrase lists.

Settlement is call-shaped; the product is still question-shaped. Clearer receipts and budgets per question would make “pay for reasoning” feel like a product.

The local layer is trusted more than it is isolated. Policy can constrain what ships; it cannot make local execution a full sandbox of an untrusted world.

docs.title: How to use this document
docs.text:
When adding a feature or changing a configured value, ask:

  1. Which layer owns it?
  2. Which steering policy does it extend or contradict?

Layer ownership:

  • If it touches the file or the result, it belongs in the local layer.
  • If it decides whether to generate, it belongs in dialogue.
  • If it produces something executable or viewable, it belongs in synthesis — not a new intent, and not a new Plan for a toggle.
  • If it is about who pays or which model runs, it belongs in settlement.

If a change requires the control plane to see more of the file, the model to pick a pipeline, a new Plan for what is really an optional artifact, or a second entry path with different semantics, it is fighting this philosophy. That can still be the right call — but it should be named as a bet change, not as a small addition.

If a change only adjusts a config value, state the direction (the table in Steering policies) so the team knows what tradeoff moved.

docs.title: Cloud API — Usage Reference
docs.text:
This document covers how to call the Cloud API endpoints, with full cURL examples and parameter references.

The Cloud API turns a natural-language question plus dataset metadata into Artifacts for local execution: Pandas code (code_pandas), an optional computation-graph DAG (dag), and an optional chart contract (visualization_spec). The Cloud API never receives the full data file.

The desktop Ask Queries path uses the conversation endpoints. Direct generate_dag endpoints exist for the same generation Capability without a chat session.

Related docs:

Doc Purpose CONVERSATION_WORKFLOW.md Desktop chat loop, intents, clarification SYSTEM_ARCHITECTURE.md Capability → Plan → Stage → Artifact TELEMETRY.md Job state, attempt logs, tokens, credit receipts CREDITS.md User-facing credits, monthly allowance, examples BILLING.md Developer billing internals AUTH_SETUP.md Portal Google/Supabase auth

docs.title: 🔐 Authentication
docs.text:
Every request to /api/v1/* or /api/v2/* must include your API key in the X-API-Key header.

-H "X-API-Key: <your-api-key>"

You obtain your API key from the Nolain portal (see CLOUD_API_USER.md and POST /api/auth/keys in AUTH_SETUP.md).

Portal account routes under /api/auth/* use a Supabase access token instead:

-H "Authorization: Bearer <access_token>"

The exception is GET /api/auth/key-status, which authenticates with X-API-Key (desktop Settings panel).

docs.title: Consumption limits
docs.text:
Consumption is account-based for portal-linked keys. Admission reads profiles_nolain_query.credit_balance and returns 402 Payment Required when the balance is empty.

Key type Admission Charged per LLM call Portal-linked (user_id set) Requires credit_balance > 0 Yes Unlinked owner (tier = owner, no user_id) Always admitted No Unlinked non-owner 402 —

Monthly plan grants (see CREDITS.md):

Tier Credits / month free 1 000 premium 50 000

Queueing a generation job does not consume credits by itself. Each LLM call is charged from token usage plus surplus as soon as it completes. Details: CREDITS.md, BILLING.md.

All LLM traffic routes through OpenRouter. Pass an optional model field (catalog id from GET /api/v1/llm/models); omit it to use the server default (deepseek-v4-flash-0731 unless overridden in llm_models.yaml).

docs.title: GET /api/v1/llm/models — Model Catalog
docs.text:
Lists selectable models and the server default. Uses authentication-only mode.

curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/llm/models \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk-your-key-here"

Response (shape):

{
  "provider": "openrouter",
  "default_model_id": "deepseek-v4-flash-0731",
  "models": [
    { "id": "deepseek-v4-flash-0731", "label": "DeepSeek V4 Flash (0731)", "openrouter_model": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731", "default": true },
    { "id": "gpt-5.6-luna", "label": "GPT-5.6 Luna", "openrouter_model": "openai/gpt-5.6-luna" }
  ]
}

docs.title: GET / — Service Status
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:8000/

Response:

{
  "app": "Data Query DAG Generator API",
  "status": "online",
  "documentation": "/docs"
}

docs.title: GET /health — Runtime Health
docs.text:
Reports Redis, Celery workers, and Supabase configuration. Generation endpoints return 503 when Redis or a Celery worker is unavailable.

curl http://localhost:8000/health

Response:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "services": {
    "redis": { "ok": true },
    "celery": { "ok": true, "workers": ["celery@host"] },
    "supabase": { "ok": true, "host": "your-project.supabase.co" }
  }
}

status is "degraded" when any listed service is not ok.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/capabilities — Capability / Plan Catalog
docs.text:
Lists registered generation Capabilities, Plans, and optional Artifacts. Intent classification is separate: optional Artifacts (DAG, visualization spec) are request options on a Plan, not extra plan ids.

Uses authentication-only mode (does not enforce remaining credits).

curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/capabilities \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk-your-key-here"

Response (shape):

{
  "capabilities": [
    {
      "id": "data_analysis",
      "enabled": true,
      "plans": [
        {
          "plan_id": "data_analysis/pandas",
          "selectable": true,
          "default": true,
          "implemented": true,
          "engine": "pandas",
          "stages": ["generate_pandas", "compile_dag", "format_visualization", "validate_visualization", "validate_dag", "finalize_plan"],
          "optional_stages": ["compile_dag", "format_visualization", "validate_visualization"],
          "optional_artifacts": ["dag", "visualization_spec"],
          "terminal_artifact_kinds": ["code_pandas", "dag", "visualization_spec"]
        },
        {
          "plan_id": "data_analysis/ibis",
          "selectable": false,
          "implemented": false
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

data_analysis/ibis is catalogued but not selectable. Legacy plan ids such as data_analysis/analysis/with_dag map to data_analysis/pandas plus options.

docs.title: POST /api/v1/analyze_query — Semantic Analysis 🧠 (Synchronous)
docs.text:
Analyzes a natural language query to detect ambiguous concepts (polysemy, granularity, vagueness) before DAG generation.

This direct endpoint charges credits for the LLM call(s) it makes. The same semantic step inside POST /api/v1/conversation/message is also charged when it invokes a model.

docs.text: Field Type Required Description query string ✅ Natural language question about your data metadata object ✅ Dataset schema info (see Metadata Object) model string ❌ Catalog model id (e.g. "deepseek-v4-flash-0731"). Default: server default from llm_models.yaml. n_interpretations int ❌ Candidate interpretations per ambiguity. Default: 4.

docs.title: Realistic Full-Featured Example

docs.title: POST /api/v2/generate_dag — data_analysis Capability (Asynchronous)
docs.text:
Admits the registered data_analysis Capability. The server builds a Plan of Stages from request options. The pandas Plan always produces a code_pandas Artifact (pandas_code on the status payload). Optional Stages add a DAG and/or a visualization spec. Each LLM call in the worker is charged as it completes; poll billing.charged_credits on the status payload for the running total.

Pandas Plan Stages (built from options):

  1. generate_pandas — LLM produces Pandas code from the query + metadata. The worker applies deterministic compatibility patches and static preflight checks (no execution on the server). Truncated (finish_reason=length), empty, syntactically invalid, unsafe, or structurally incomplete code is rejected before delivery and may retry under the adaptive repair policy.
  2. compile_dag — optional (compile_dag=true, default); LLM translates the code into a DAG
  3. format_visualization — optional (include_visualization=true, default); LLM produces a visualization_spec
  4. validate_visualization — optional (when include_visualization=true); validates the chart contract
  5. validate_dag — optional (when compile_dag=true); validates the DAG
  6. finalize_plan — mark success (no separate charge; billing is per LLM call)

descriptive / visualization / transformation are not Capabilities or Plans. Charts set include_visualization; they do not change plan_id.

Poll responses include capability_id, plan_id, current_stage, compile_dag, include_visualization, pandas_code, optional graph / visualization_spec, and an optional artifacts[] envelope. Pandas reliability fields are:

  • pandas_retries_left: remaining local-runtime repair jobs
  • pandas_sandbox_retries_left: remaining in-cloud retries
  • pandas_attempts_used / pandas_total_max_attempts: chain usage and ceiling
  • generation_attempts: bounded diagnostics for each LLM call, including finish reason, selected policy profile, token counts, and outcome

docs.title: POST /api/v1/conversation/result
docs.text:
Notify the server of local execution so follow-ups have context. No charge on a successful store.

When exec_error and pandas_code are set, the previous generation job succeeded, that job still has pandas_retries_left > 0, and the chain has not reached pandas_total_max_attempts, the server queues a generate_pandas repair job (same query, failed code + traceback, no classifier). Jobs that already failed in the cloud (syntax/sandbox rejects) are not re-queued as runtime repairs. It carries attempt history forward and resets the sandbox retry budget for the repair job, then returns:

{
  "status": "repairing",
  "type": "generation",
  "task_id": "...",
  "session_id": "...",
  "capability_id": "data_analysis",
  "plan_id": "data_analysis/pandas",
  "compile_dag": true,
  "include_visualization": true,
  "pandas_retries_left": 1
}

Poll that task_id and re-execute locally. If no retries remain, the response is { "status": "ok" }.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/conversation/result \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk-your-key-here" \
  -d '{
    "session_id": "c0a1b2c3-d4e5-6789-abcd-ef1234567890",
    "dag": { "graph_id": "...", "nodes": [], "output_node": "node_2" },
    "exec_result": { "preview": [{"Country": "United Kingdom", "revenue": 912345.0}] },
    "pandas_code": "result = df.groupby('Country')['Quantity'].sum()"
  }'
